findings.quote: Dapat ding akma ang buong parirala sa sinasabi ng pangungusap.
findings.problem: Parirala is a Filipino grammar term used without the required English gloss on first use. Pang-ugnay has its connector gloss, but parirala has no corresponding phrase gloss anywhere in this lesson.

checked: Examples 14–16 have Filipino stems, sample sentences, choices and explanatory solution prose. Examples 1–13 belong to the separate English portion.

checked: The Filipino section uses Filipino teaching prose. The single connector gloss is required terminology support; no unnecessary English words are mixed into its sentences.

L14.note: No example asks about a target word in a supplied sentence; these are completion tasks, not bold-word meaning questions.

checked: The summary directly names the completion clues. No banned stock phrase appears, and the teaching paragraphs vary their sentence openings.

The Language Proficiency layout uses Core Concept, Examples, Speed Tricks & Shortcuts, and Traps to Watch For, which is permitted. No worked example uses a mathematical formula; the formula-before-example requirement has no formula instance here.
Mapped distinct meaning cases: contrast #1, cause/result #2, interacting blanks #3, illustration #12, and idiom #13.
Mapped grammar and usage cases: main verb/word form #4, agreement #5, earlier/ongoing past #6, verb complements #7, collocation #8, preposition #9, articles/context #10, parallel list #11.

Filipino contextual time/form #14, linking meaning #15, and natural word combination #16 cover the added Filipino completion facet. Examples move from direct meaning clues to combined choices. No brief-required completion case remains absent.

checked: Checked teaching and trap paragraphs for the one-to-three-sentence limit. Multi-step reasoning is in numbered lists, and there are no long bullet lists.

checked: Word form, noun, adjective and adverb are defined before their application. Agreement is introduced with singular/plural sentence pairs. Past participle and the three past constructions are explained before Example 6.
Countable noun, a/an sounds, contextual the, prepositions, parallel structure, collocation and idiom each get local meaning and examples before the worked tasks.

The Filipino section explains linking words through reason, result and contrast and gives natural word combinations. No finite verb terminology remains. Parirala lacks its English gloss under L09, but its ordinary phrase meaning is shown by the adjacent combinations malaking tulong and matinding ulan.
Meaning clues explain the links they signal and require checking both ideas. Word-form teaching explains the job of a blank rather than only naming grammar categories.

Agreement, past forms, verb complements, articles and prepositions each show how a completion is selected. Parallel structure demonstrates shared -ing forms; collocation and idiom show whole expressions and their meanings.
Filipino instruction links a past-time cue to completed action, explains dahil/kaya/ngunit, and demonstrates natural combinations. Examples 14–16 apply these checks.
The lesson warns against deciding from a signal word alone or solving only one blank. Each completed sentence must fit both meaning and grammar.
Past perfect is limited to making an earlier past action clear, and simple past may be enough for a finished event. Verb-complement patterns must be learned with the governing verb.

A/an applies to one countable item not already identified and is chosen by sound. The applies when context identifies the referent. Prepositions depend on fixed phrase and intended meaning; matching forms apply to items doing the same job.
